SR Pal, Senior Advocate, instructed by Shamsul Haque Siddique Advocate-on-Record — For the Appellant.
Md. Abdur Rahim, Advocate-on-Record — For the Respondent.
parties:
Mokbul Hossain Khandker (Md) ----- Appellant
Vs.
Jaheda Khatun ----- Respondent
full_judgment:
2. The plaintiff-respondent filed SCC Suit No. 24 of 1982 in the SCC Court and the learned Subordinate Judge, Bogra for eviction of the appellant from the suit land and for a decree for Taka 360.00 as arrear rent. The appellant took on rent a stall room from the respondent at a monthly rent of Taka 10.00 by a registered deed of agreement to be effective for 5 years from 1 -11-65. The respondent expressed her intention to construct pucca stalls on the suit land and at the request of the appellant orally agreed that he would be allowed to pay monthly rent as before till the construction work is commenced. Towards the end of 1970 the respondent's husband stored 90,000 bricks and 50 cubic feet of sand on the vacant site of Rafique Khan Market on which the appellant's stall was situated. The appellant continued to pay rent up to February. 1971, although irregularly. The entire market was set on fire and some parts of some stalls were damaged. The respondent's husband was a Muslim Leaguer and a member of the peace committee as well as a candidate for by-election as an MPA and therefore after liberation of Bangladesh he went into hiding. For and on behalf of the respondent her minor sons could not look after the suit property. Taking advantage of that situation the appellant constructed a pucca two-storied structure on the suit land using the materials stored by the respondent's husband. After the Government announced general amnesty towards the end of 1974 the respondent's husband returned to Bogra Town and asked explanation from the appellant in respect of the construction and demanded rent from him which the appellant avoided to pay on some pretext or other. Hence the suit for eviction and the claim for arrear rent from 1979 to 1981, in total for Taka 360.00 

 3. The appellant in his written statement denied the respondent's case and claimed that the suit land belonged to one Ekram Hossain Tarafder and others with a dilapidated building thereon. When the building cola-passed a market called Badruddin New Market was established on the western side of the vacant land by enterprising businessmen on two sides of the road using tin and wood for construction. Similar markets were established on both sides of the road near Bogra Thana and Station Road. The road side stall keepers were evicted under the Martial Law of 1958 and the businessmen shifted their business to the vacant suit land. The respondent's husband claiming to be the owner of the suit land asked for explanation from the owners of the stalls. The stall owners asked for the permission of the husband of the respondent to continue their business to which he agreed. Hence from the end of October 1958 the appellant constructed a wooden and tin stall measuring 5"x5" and started the business of selling clothes therein. The vacant land thus gradually turned into a market. As a consideration for the permissive occupation of the stalls the husband of the respondent demanded a fee from the stall owners depending on the size of their respective stalls in the early part of October.1965. The appellant and the other stall owners agreed to pay him Taka 2.00 per feet as license fee. But for purpose of registering a document in this connection the respondent's husband engaged a moharar of his own choice and converted a document of permissive possession into a registered document of tenancy. The appellant also purchased another stall from another stall owner and as such he became the owner and possessor of two stalls. Upon the outbreak of liberation war all the stalls of the said market were set on fire by Pak Army and the appellant's stalls were completely gutted. As such the permissive possession of the appellant came to an end. After liberation the appellant came to know that the suit land was declared as an abandoned property. The Government orally permitted the stall owners including the appellant to construct necessary structures and re-start their business. The appellant in co-operation with other stall owners purchased bricks, sand, iron rods, cement at their own costs and constructed the present two-storied building on the suit land at his own cost and has been conducting his business since 1972 therein in his own right. The appellant denied the relationship of landlord and tenant between him and the respondent and asserted that the respondent has no right, title and interest in the suit land. 

 4. The SCC Court found that the respondent was the owner of the suit land and the appellant was a tenant under her by virtue of a registered deed of agreement for lease and that he paid rent to the respondent up to February, 1971. The appellant is a defaulter thereafter. He cannot raise the question of title of the landlord in an SCC suit. As the appellant agreed that he would continue as a tenant if a new construction is made and as the appellant did not surrender the suit land to the respondent after the stalls were destroyed by fire the relationship of landlord and tenant still continues. The SCC Court came to a finding from the evidence of PWs 4 and 6 that the appellant constructed the pucca two-storied stalls with the materials stored by the respondent's husband in the vacant land of the market. On these findings the SCC Court decreed the suit. 

 7. The sum and substance of the submissions of Mr. SR Pal, learned Advocate for the appellant is that, after reviewing a number of cases of this sub-continent as well as the English case of national Carriers Ltd. vs. Panalpina (1981) 2 WLR 45 this Division in the afore-cited case reported in 36 DLR (AD) 195 held that the doctrine of frustration as embodied in section 56 of the Contract Act is applicable to leases of immovable property. The said case is therefore fully applicable to the facts of the present case and the High Court Division made an erroneous distinction between the facts of the present case and the cited case. The suit stalls were admittedly gutted by fire in March, 1971 and after a lapse of one year the appellant made the puce construction in 1972. There was thus a gap of one year during which the appellant was not in possession of the suit land. The tenancy came to an end in March, 1971 by the application of the doctrine of frustration and the appellant's assumption of the suit land and construction thereon in 1972 must therefore be construed to be an unauthorized possession and construction of structures. The remedy of the respondent, if any, was to file a suit for declaration of title and restoration of possession of the respondent claiming mesne profits, and in any view of the matter the SCC suit is not maintainable. 

 8. Mr. Md. Abdur Rahim learned Advocate-on-Record for the respondent, submits that the issue of forum was not raised nor any issue on forum was framed in the SCC Court. It was raised for the first time before the High Court Division in Revision. The appellant did not leave the suit land from March, 1971 to 1972 when he constructed a two-storied pucca stall and it is the finding of the SCC Court with which the High Court Division concurred that he made the pucca construction with the materials left by the respondent's husband. The appellant did not offer back the possession of the suit land to the respondent when it was gutted by fire. Mr. Rahim relies upon the case of Golam Rahman vs. Mrs. Imratunnessa. 22 DLR 126 and submits that under section 108(e) of the Transfer of Property Act the tenant has to avoid the lease even when the subject matter of the lease is completely destroyed by fire. The respondent did not avoid the lease by any notice. Further, he submits, the respondent submitted an application to the District Judge. Bogra under section 28A of the Small Causes Court Act for converting the SCC suit into a regular suit and for its transfer to an appropriate civil Court in view of the question of title raised by the appellant even though evidence given by the two sides was complete and the SCC suit was at that time pending for argument The appellant opposed that application and submitted that the SCC Court was competent to decide whether the appellant was a tenant under the respondent or a permissive occupier and that there was no complicated question of title involved in it. The learned District Judge accepted the submissions of the appellant and rejected the conversion and transfer application of the respondent. Now it does not lie in the mouth of the appellant to contend that the SCC Court had no jurisdiction to try the suit and that the suit ought to have been filed for a declaration of title and recovery of possession with mesne profit. 

 9. We have perused the written statement of the appellant very minutely. All that the appellant contended therein by way of claiming any manner of frustration of the contract is that after the appellant's stalls were completely gutted by fire by the Pak Army his permissive possession under the respondent or her husband came to end. The frustration of a contract of lease is a mixed question of law and fact. The appellant failed to allege frustration of lease, both on facts and law. He misdirected his defence towards a different course compelling the respondent to prove lease, not license No issue on frustration was framed by the SCC Court. In the case of Azizur Rahman vs. Abdus Sakur 36 DLR (AD) 195, on which Mr. SR Pal relies, it is the plaintiff who claimed that the tenancy was destroyed by fire and the relationship of landlord and tenant came to an end. The suit premises remained vacant and in possession of the plaintiffs. The defendants in collusion with each other and ignoring the plaintiffs' protest and also his lawyer's notice wrongfully reconstructed new huts and houses on the suit premises and refused to deliver possession of the suit land to the plaintiffs. So the plaintiff filed a suit for declaration of title and recovery of possession. It was the defence of the defendants that there was no extinction of the subject matter of tenancy due to the conflagration. The defendants were continuing as monthly tenants in respect of the suit premises. This Division held, after a review of various cases of the sub-continent and a case from the English jurisdiction that the doctrine of frustration, as embodied in section 56 of the Contract Act, is applicable to leases of immovable property. The plaintiff's suit for declaration of title and recovery of possession was held to be maintainable in the circumstance. The defendant-appellant's contention that the tenancy subsists was not accepted. 

 10. The High Court Division, it appears, accepting fully the ratio decidendi of the afore-cited case in 36 DLR (AD) 195, sought to make a distinction between the facts of the said case and the present case. It rightly found that in the present case the respondent as plaintiff did not resume possession of the suit land after the stalls were gutted by fire in March, 1971. There is no averment and no claim on the part of the appellant that after the fire he left the suit land. He held on to it and did not deliver up vacant possession of the suit land to the respondent. He constructed a puce two-storied stall on the suit land with the materials purchased and stored by the plaintiff's husband. He continued to occupy the suit land on the new stalls as a tenant of the appellant, under a previously agreed oral agreement. In such circumstances, the High Court Division rightly held, the appellant cannot say that he is not a tenant and cannot claim title either. 

 11. Although we have no reason to depart from our decision reported in 36 DLR (AD) 195 we are of the opinion that the appellant cannot be permitted to take advantage of the doctrine of frustration in the peculiar facts and circumstances of the present case. Had he pleaded frustration of a contract of lease fairly and squarely in the written statement, the plaintiff would have had an opportunity to meet that defence by leading evidence. On the contrary his defence was one of denial of the plaintiff's title, then one of permissive possession, then extinction of permissive possession by fire and thereafter possession of the structures in his own right and title. Frustration of a contract of lease was pleaded specifically and pointedly only at the revisional stage in the High Court Division. Advantage was sought to be taken of the fact that there was a gap of one year during which the suit land was lying vacant after the fire and it was argued that the appellant could not be said to be continuing in possession during the said period of one year. Had the defendant specifically pleaded in his written statement that he was not in possession of the suit land after the fire and that he re-entered the suit land after one year against the opposition of the plaintiff and constructed pucca stalls forcibly therein, the plaintiff-respondent would have had an opportunity to lead evidence that the appellant never left the possession of the suit land. Besides, the appellant too has neither stated in his written statement nor has led evidence that he left the suit land or handed over the possession of the same to the plaintiff after his stalls were gutted by fire. Furthermore, the plaintiff-respondent had taken steps to take the suit out of the SCC Court for trial as a regular title suit and it is the appellant who successfully resisted that attempt. Now to ask the respondent to file a regular suit for declaration of title and recovery of possession will be tantamount to putting a premium on the appellant's desperate and contradictory stands. We, therefore, find that there was no misinterpretation of section 108(e) of the Transfer of Property Act and section 56 of the Contract Act by the High Court Division and the case reported in 36 DLR (AD) 195 was rightly distinguished.
